title: Licensing Conditions
description: Understanding UK amateur radio licence types, Ofcom regulations, callsigns, permitted bands, power limits, and operating conditions.
content:
UK Amateur Radio Licensing

Amateur radio in the United Kingdom is regulated by Ofcom (the Office of Communications). To transmit on amateur radio frequencies, you must hold a valid amateur radio licence. There are three progressive licence levels:

Licence LevelCallsign PrefixMax Power (PEP)Exam Required
FoundationM710 WattsFoundation
Intermediate2E0 / 2E150 WattsFoundation + Intermediate
FullM0 / M1400 WattsFoundation + Intermediate + Full

Callsign Structure

Your callsign is your unique identifier on the air. A UK Foundation callsign follows the format:

M7 + three letters (e.g., M7ABC)

The prefix tells other operators your licence class and country. Additional prefixes are used in different UK nations:

  • MW7 — Wales
  • MM7 — Scotland
  • MI7 — Northern Ireland

When operating from a location different to your main station address, you may need to add a regional secondary locator, such as /M for mobile, /P for portable, or /MM for maritime mobile.

Foundation Licence Bands and Power

As a Foundation licence holder, you are permitted to operate on specific amateur radio bands with a maximum transmitter power of 10 Watts PEP (Peak Envelope Power). The key bands available include:

  • HF Bands: 80m (3.5 MHz), 40m (7 MHz), 30m (10 MHz), 20m (14 MHz), 17m (18 MHz), 15m (21 MHz), 10m (28 MHz)
  • VHF: 2m (144 MHz)
  • UHF: 70cm (430 MHz)

Operating Conditions

Key conditions of the Foundation licence include:

  • You must keep a log of all transmissions, recording date, time (UTC), frequency/band, mode, callsign of station worked, and signal reports exchanged
  • You must identify your station by transmitting your callsign at regular intervals
  • You must not cause undue interference to other radio users or electronic equipment
  • You must operate within your permitted frequency bands and power limits
  • You must not transmit music, advertisements, or encrypted messages (except for certain digital modes)
  • You must not use your radio for business purposes
  • Third-party messages are permitted but you remain responsible for the content

Ofcom and the Licence

Ofcom is the independent regulator for UK communications industries. They:

  • Issue amateur radio licences (currently free of charge)
  • Allocate frequency bands for amateur use
  • Investigate interference complaints
  • Can revoke licences for serious breaches

The licence is issued under the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006. You must be at least no minimum age to hold a Foundation licence — people of any age can obtain one.

Study Tips

For the exam, make sure you know: the three licence levels and their power limits, the Foundation callsign format (M7 + 3 letters), that Ofcom is the regulator, the requirement to keep a log, and the key operating conditions listed above.

title: Technical Basics
description: Fundamental electronics: voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's Law, power, AC/DC, frequency, wavelength, and decibels.
content:
Electricity Fundamentals

Understanding basic electrical concepts is essential for amateur radio. There are three fundamental quantities:

  • Voltage (V) — the electrical pressure or 'push' that drives current through a circuit, measured in Volts (V)
  • Current (I) — the flow of electrical charge, measured in Amperes (A)
  • Resistance (R) — opposition to current flow, measured in Ohms (Ω)

Ohm's Law

Ohm's Law describes the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance:

V = I × R

This can be rearranged to find any of the three values:

  • V = I × R (Voltage = Current × Resistance)
  • I = V / R (Current = Voltage ÷ Resistance)
  • R = V / I (Resistance = Voltage ÷ Current)

Example: A 12V battery connected across a 4Ω resistor: I = 12 / 4 = 3 Amperes

Electrical Power

Power is the rate at which electrical energy is used or produced, measured in Watts (W):

P = V × I

Combined with Ohm's Law, we also get:

  • P = I² × R
  • P = V² / R

Example: A Foundation station running 10W into a 50Ω load: I = √(P/R) = √(10/50) = √0.2 ≈ 0.45A

Series and Parallel Circuits

Resistors in Series

Total resistance is the sum of individual resistances:

Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3

Resistors in Parallel

The reciprocal of total resistance equals the sum of reciprocals:

1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3

For two equal resistors in parallel: Rtotal = R / 2

AC and DC

  • DC (Direct Current) — flows in one direction only (e.g., batteries)
  • AC (Alternating Current) — reverses direction periodically (e.g., mains supply, radio signals)

AC is described by its frequency — the number of complete cycles per second, measured in Hertz (Hz). UK mains electricity is 50 Hz.

Frequency and Wavelength

Radio waves travel at the speed of light: c = 300,000,000 m/s (approximately). The relationship between frequency and wavelength is:

λ = c / f

Where λ (lambda) is wavelength in metres, c is the speed of light, and f is frequency in Hz.

Example: The 2-metre band: f = 300,000,000 / 2 = 150 MHz (actual band is 144-146 MHz)

Band NameApproximate FrequencyWavelength
80 metres3.5 MHz~86m
40 metres7 MHz~43m
20 metres14 MHz~21m
2 metres144 MHz~2.1m
70 centimetres430 MHz~70cm

Decibels (dB)

Decibels express ratios on a logarithmic scale. Key values to remember:

  • +3 dB = double the power
  • -3 dB = half the power
  • +10 dB = ten times the power
  • -10 dB = one-tenth of the power
  • +6 dB ≈ double the voltage

Example: An amplifier that changes a 1W signal to 2W provides a gain of +3 dB

Metric Prefixes

PrefixSymbolMultiplier
MegaM× 1,000,000
kilok× 1,000
millim× 0.001
microμ× 0.000001

Study Tips

You MUST know Ohm's Law and the power formula for the exam. Practice quick calculations. Remember: 3 dB = double power, 10 dB = ten times power. Know the wavelength formula λ = c/f.

title: Transmitters and Receivers
description: How radio transmitters and receivers work: oscillators, modulators, amplifiers, mixers, IF stages, and modulation types.
content:
The Transmitter

A radio transmitter converts information (voice, data, Morse code) into radio frequency signals that can be radiated from an antenna. The basic building blocks are:

  1. Oscillator — generates a stable radio frequency (RF) signal at the desired operating frequency
  2. Modulator — imposes information onto the RF signal by varying its amplitude, frequency, or phase
  3. Amplifier — increases the power of the signal to the desired output level
  4. Filter — removes unwanted signals and harmonics before the signal reaches the antenna

The Receiver

A radio receiver extracts information from incoming radio signals. Most modern receivers use the superheterodyne (superhet) principle:

  1. Antenna picks up radio signals
  2. RF Amplifier — amplifies the weak incoming signal
  3. Mixer — combines the incoming signal with a local oscillator to produce an Intermediate Frequency (IF)
  4. IF Amplifier and Filter — amplifies and selects just the wanted signal at the IF frequency
  5. Demodulator (Detector) — extracts the original information from the IF signal
  6. Audio Amplifier — amplifies the audio signal to drive a speaker or headphones

Modulation Types

Modulation is the process of varying a radio signal to carry information. The main types used in amateur radio are:

AM (Amplitude Modulation)

  • The amplitude (strength) of the carrier is varied according to the audio signal
  • Simple but inefficient — uses more bandwidth and power than necessary
  • The carrier itself contains no information

FM (Frequency Modulation)

  • The frequency of the carrier is varied according to the audio signal
  • Better audio quality and more resistant to noise than AM
  • Widely used on VHF and UHF (e.g., 2m and 70cm FM repeaters)
  • Uses more bandwidth than SSB

SSB (Single Sideband)

  • A form of AM where the carrier and one sideband are removed, transmitting only one sideband
  • Much more efficient use of power and bandwidth
  • USB (Upper Sideband) — used on frequencies above 10 MHz
  • LSB (Lower Sideband) — used on frequencies below 10 MHz
  • The most common mode for HF voice communication

CW (Continuous Wave / Morse Code)

  • Simplest mode — the carrier is keyed on and off to send Morse code
  • Very narrow bandwidth, works well with weak signals
  • Not required for Foundation licence but good to understand

Key Receiver Concepts

  • Sensitivity — the ability to receive weak signals. A more sensitive receiver can detect weaker signals.
  • Selectivity — the ability to separate the wanted signal from nearby unwanted signals. Better selectivity means you can distinguish closely-spaced signals.
  • Bandwidth — the range of frequencies passed by a filter. Narrower bandwidth improves selectivity but must be wide enough for the mode in use.
ModeTypical Bandwidth
CW500 Hz
SSB2.4 kHz
AM6 kHz
FM (narrow)12.5 kHz
FM (wide)25 kHz

Transceiver

Most amateur radio equipment is a transceiver — a combined transmitter and receiver in one unit. When you press the PTT (Push-To-Talk) switch, it switches from receive to transmit mode.

Study Tips

Know the block diagrams of a basic transmitter and superhet receiver. Understand the difference between AM, FM, and SSB. Remember that SSB is most efficient for HF voice, FM is used on VHF/UHF. Know what sensitivity and selectivity mean.

title: Feeders and Antennas
description: Coaxial cable, impedance, SWR, antenna types (dipole, vertical, Yagi), polarisation, baluns, and antenna tuning units.
content:
Feeders (Transmission Lines)

A feeder (or transmission line) connects your transceiver to the antenna. The most common type in amateur radio is coaxial cable (coax).

Coaxial Cable

Coax consists of:

  • A central inner conductor
  • Surrounded by insulating dielectric
  • Covered by a braided outer conductor (screen/shield)
  • Protected by an outer jacket

Common types include:

TypeImpedanceLossUse
RG-5850ΩHigherShort runs, HF
RG-21350ΩLowerGeneral purpose
Westflex 10350ΩVery lowVHF/UHF, longer runs
RG-7575ΩMediumTV systems (not amateur)

Characteristic Impedance

Every feeder has a characteristic impedance, measured in Ohms. For amateur radio, the standard is 50Ω. The impedance depends on the physical dimensions and materials of the cable, not its length.

Standing Wave Ratio (SWR)

SWR measures how well the antenna impedance matches the feeder impedance. A perfect match gives an SWR of 1:1.

  • SWR 1:1 — perfect match, all power reaches the antenna
  • SWR 1.5:1 — good, very little power reflected
  • SWR 2:1 — acceptable, some power reflected
  • SWR 3:1 or higher — poor match, significant power reflected back to the transmitter

High SWR means power is being reflected back down the feeder, which wastes power and can damage the transmitter. An SWR meter is used to measure the SWR.

Common Antenna Types

Dipole

  • The most basic antenna — two equal-length conductors fed at the centre
  • A half-wave dipole for a given frequency has a total length of approximately λ/2 (half a wavelength)
  • Feed point impedance is approximately 73Ω (close enough to 50Ω for practical use)
  • Radiates broadside to the wire (perpendicular to the wire's length)
  • Example: a half-wave dipole for the 2m band is about 1 metre long (each half ≈ 50cm)

Vertical (Ground Plane)

  • A quarter-wave vertical element with ground plane radials
  • Radiates equally in all horizontal directions (omnidirectional)
  • Good for VHF/UHF and for making contacts in all directions
  • Feed point impedance approximately 36Ω (often matched with a transformer)

Yagi-Uda (Yagi)

  • A directional antenna with multiple elements: one driven element, one reflector, and one or more directors
  • Provides gain in the forward direction — concentrates the signal
  • More elements = more gain and a narrower beam
  • Used for VHF/UHF DX (long-distance) contacts and satellite work
  • Must be pointed towards the station you want to communicate with

Polarisation

The polarisation of an antenna refers to the orientation of the electric field:

  • Horizontal — the element is horizontal (e.g., a horizontal dipole). Used for HF and SSB on VHF.
  • Vertical — the element is vertical (e.g., a vertical antenna). Used for VHF/UHF FM.

For best results, both stations should use the same polarisation. A mismatch causes significant signal loss (up to 20 dB).

Baluns

A balun (balanced-to-unbalanced) is used when connecting a balanced antenna (like a dipole) to an unbalanced feeder (like coax). It prevents unwanted currents flowing on the outside of the coax, which can cause interference and radiation pattern distortion.

Antenna Tuning Unit (ATU)

An ATU (Antenna Tuning Unit) transforms the impedance at the end of the feeder to match the transceiver's 50Ω output. It does NOT make the antenna more efficient — it simply provides a match so the transmitter can deliver full power. The losses in the feeder between the ATU and antenna remain.

Study Tips

Know that amateur radio uses 50Ω coax. Understand SWR (1:1 is perfect). Know the three main antenna types and their characteristics. Remember horizontal polarisation for SSB, vertical for FM. Understand what a balun does and what an ATU does (and doesn't do).

title: Propagation
description: How radio waves travel: ground wave, sky wave, ionosphere layers, line of sight, VHF/UHF and HF propagation characteristics.
content:
How Radio Waves Travel

Radio waves can travel from transmitter to receiver by several different paths, depending on the frequency and conditions. Understanding propagation helps you know which bands to use and when.

Ground Wave

Ground wave propagation follows the surface of the Earth. It is most effective at lower frequencies (below about 2 MHz). The wave follows the curvature of the Earth, allowing communication beyond the visible horizon. Ground wave range depends on:

  • Transmitter power
  • Frequency (lower frequencies travel further)
  • Ground conductivity (sea water is best)

At HF amateur frequencies, ground wave range is typically limited to a few tens of kilometres.

Sky Wave (Ionospheric Propagation)

Sky wave propagation occurs when radio waves are refracted (bent) back to Earth by the ionosphere — layers of ionised gas in the upper atmosphere. This enables long-distance HF communication across hundreds or thousands of kilometres.

Ionosphere Layers

LayerHeightCharacteristics
D Layer60-90 kmOnly present during daytime. Absorbs HF signals (especially lower HF). Disappears at night, improving HF propagation.
E Layer100-120 kmPresent during daytime. Can refract signals. Sporadic E can occur, enabling unusual VHF propagation.
F1 Layer150-220 kmPresent during daytime. Merges with F2 at night.
F2 Layer250-400 kmMost important for HF propagation. Present day and night. Responsible for most long-distance HF contacts.

Key Sky Wave Concepts

  • Skip Distance — the minimum distance at which sky wave signals return to Earth. There is a 'dead zone' between the end of ground wave range and the start of sky wave reception.
  • Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) — the highest frequency that will be refracted back to Earth for a given path. Above the MUF, signals pass through the ionosphere into space. The MUF varies with time of day, season, and solar activity.
  • Critical Frequency — the highest frequency that is reflected when transmitted vertically upward. The MUF for an oblique path is always higher than the critical frequency.

Solar Activity

The ionosphere is created by solar radiation ionising atmospheric gases. Solar activity follows an approximately 11-year cycle:

  • Solar maximum — higher MUF, better conditions for higher HF bands (10m, 15m, 20m)
  • Solar minimum — lower MUF, higher bands may not be usable, lower bands (40m, 80m) more reliable

Line of Sight (VHF/UHF Propagation)

At VHF (30-300 MHz) and UHF (300 MHz - 3 GHz), signals generally travel in straight lines, similar to light. This means range is normally limited to the visual horizon plus a bit further (due to slight refraction in the atmosphere).

Range can be increased by:

  • Using higher antenna positions (hilltops, tall masts)
  • Using directional antennas (Yagi) with gain
  • Using repeaters on high ground

Special VHF/UHF Propagation

  • Sporadic E — Occasional patches of intense ionisation in the E layer can reflect VHF signals over hundreds of kilometres. Unpredictable but exciting.
  • Tropospheric Ducting — Temperature inversions in the lower atmosphere can guide VHF/UHF signals over long distances. Most common in summer.
  • Rain Scatter — At UHF and microwave frequencies, signals can be scattered by heavy rain, enabling contacts in unusual directions.

Study Tips

Know the ionosphere layers (D absorbs, F2 is most important for HF). Understand that HF uses sky wave while VHF/UHF is normally line of sight. Know what MUF means. Remember that the D layer disappears at night, improving HF propagation on lower bands.

title: EMC (Electromagnetic Compatibility)
description: Understanding interference, breakthrough, harmonics, filtering, screening, and dealing with EMC issues.
content:
What is EMC?

Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) is the ability of electronic equipment to operate without causing or suffering from electromagnetic interference. As a radio amateur, you must ensure your station doesn't interfere with other equipment, and deal with any interference you might receive.

Types of Interference

Breakthrough (Transmitted Interference)

This occurs when your transmitter signal is picked up by nearby electronic equipment such as:

  • Televisions
  • Hi-fi systems and speakers
  • Telephones
  • Computers and monitors
  • Baby monitors

Breakthrough happens because the affected equipment cannot reject the strong nearby radio signal. It is NOT necessarily a fault with your station — the affected equipment may lack adequate filtering.

Harmonics

A harmonic is a signal at a multiple of the fundamental (operating) frequency:

  • If transmitting on 7 MHz (40m), the 2nd harmonic is at 14 MHz
  • The 3rd harmonic is at 21 MHz

Harmonics can cause interference to other services. They are reduced by using a low-pass filter on the transmitter output.

Spurious Emissions

Unwanted signals other than harmonics, such as mixer products. Good transmitter design and filtering minimise these.

Reducing Interference

At Your Station

  • Use a low-pass filter on the transmitter output to reduce harmonics
  • Ensure good earthing (RF ground)
  • Keep coax connectors clean and properly fitted
  • Use the minimum power necessary for the contact
  • Ensure your antenna has a good SWR match
  • Use screened cables where possible

At the Affected Equipment

  • Ferrite chokes on cables to block RF entering the equipment
  • Band-pass or high-pass filters on TV aerial leads
  • Moving the affected equipment further from the antenna
  • Ensuring the affected equipment has proper screening

Dealing with EMC Complaints

If a neighbour reports interference:

  1. Be polite and cooperative — good relations are essential
  2. Investigate — determine if the interference is actually from your station (stop transmitting and see if the problem stops)
  3. Keep records — note the times, frequencies, and modes you were using
  4. Offer help — suggest fitting ferrite chokes or filters to the affected equipment
  5. Contact the RSGB EMC Committee for advice if needed
  6. Ofcom can investigate if the matter cannot be resolved amicably

Good EMC Practice

  • Use only properly designed and built equipment
  • Maintain your station in good condition
  • Keep your antenna system well-matched and efficient
  • Use the minimum power needed for the contact
  • Be aware of your neighbours' equipment and potential issues
  • Consider antenna placement to minimise signals towards neighbouring properties

Interference to Your Station

Your receiver may also suffer interference from nearby electrical equipment (switch-mode power supplies, LED lights, PLT/BPL devices, electric fences). If so:

  • Try to identify the source
  • Speak politely to the owner
  • Consider improving your antenna system to reject local noise

Study Tips

Know the difference between breakthrough and harmonics. Understand that ferrite chokes and filters can help. Remember to use minimum power and maintain good SWR. Know the proper procedure for dealing with interference complaints.

title: Operating Practices and Procedures
description: Phonetic alphabet, Q-codes, RST signal reports, calling procedures, repeaters, CTCSS, band plans, and contest operating.
content:
The Phonetic Alphabet

The NATO/ICAO phonetic alphabet is used to spell out callsigns and other important words clearly:

LetterWordLetterWord
AAlphaNNovember
BBravoOOscar
CCharliePPapa
DDeltaQQuebec
EEchoRRomeo
FFoxtrotSSierra
GGolfTTango
HHotelUUniform
IIndiaVVictor
JJulietWWhiskey
KKiloXX-ray
LLimaYYankee
MMikeZZulu

Q-Codes

Q-codes are three-letter abbreviations used as shorthand in amateur radio. The most important ones for Foundation are:

CodeMeaning (as question)Meaning (as statement)
QRZWho is calling me?You are being called by...
QTHWhat is your location?My location is...
QSLCan you acknowledge receipt?I acknowledge receipt
QRMAre you being interfered with?I am being interfered with (man-made)
QRNAre you troubled by static?I am troubled by static (natural noise)
QSYShall I change frequency?Change frequency to...
QRVAre you ready?I am ready
QSBAre my signals fading?Your signals are fading

RST Signal Reporting

Signal reports use the RST system:

  • R — Readability (1-5): 1 = unreadable, 5 = perfectly readable
  • S — Strength (1-9): 1 = faint, 9 = extremely strong
  • T — Tone (1-9): Only used for CW (Morse). 1 = very rough, 9 = perfect tone

For voice (phone) contacts, only R and S are used. A report of 59 means perfectly readable, extremely strong. A report of 35 means readable with difficulty, moderate signal.

Making a Call

Calling CQ (General Call)

To invite anyone to reply: "CQ CQ CQ, this is Mike Seven Alpha Bravo Charlie, Mike Seven Alpha Bravo Charlie, calling CQ and standing by."

Responding to a CQ Call

"Golf Zero Alpha Bravo Charlie, this is Mike Seven X-ray Yankee Zulu, Mike Seven X-ray Yankee Zulu, over."

During a Contact (QSO)

  • Exchange callsigns, signal reports, names, and QTH (location)
  • Use 'over' to indicate you've finished speaking and expect a reply
  • Use 'out' (or '73') at the end of the contact — never use 'over and out'!
  • 73 = best wishes (not 'seventy-threes' — just '73')

Repeaters

A repeater is an automated station, usually on a hilltop, that receives signals on one frequency and simultaneously retransmits them on another. This extends the range of low-power stations.

  • The input frequency is where you transmit (the repeater receives)
  • The output frequency is where you listen (the repeater transmits)
  • The difference is called the shift (e.g., -600 kHz on 2m)

CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System)

Many repeaters require a CTCSS tone to be transmitted along with your voice. This low-frequency tone (below 300 Hz) opens the repeater's squelch. Without the correct tone, the repeater won't respond. Your radio must be programmed with the correct CTCSS tone for each repeater.

Simplex vs Duplex

  • Simplex — transmitting and receiving on the same frequency. Used for direct station-to-station contacts.
  • Duplex — transmitting and receiving on different frequencies. Used when accessing repeaters.

Band Plans

Band plans allocate different parts of each amateur band for different modes and activities. They are agreed voluntarily (not legally enforced) but following them is good practice and prevents interference between different modes. For example, on 2m:

  • 144.000 - 144.150 MHz: CW
  • 144.150 - 144.400 MHz: SSB
  • 145.500 MHz: FM calling frequency
  • 145.600 - 145.7875 MHz: Repeater inputs

Study Tips

Learn the phonetic alphabet and key Q-codes (especially QRZ, QTH, QSL, QRM, QRN, QSY). Know the RST system. Understand how repeaters work, including shift and CTCSS. Know the difference between simplex and duplex.

title: Safety
description: Electrical safety, RF exposure limits, antenna safety, lightning protection, first aid, and safe operating practices.
content:
Electrical Safety

Electricity can kill. Even relatively low voltages can be lethal under the right conditions. As a radio amateur, you must take electrical safety very seriously.

Mains Electricity

  • UK mains supply is 230V AC at 50 Hz — this is potentially lethal
  • Always use properly rated fuses and circuit breakers
  • Never work on live equipment — switch off and unplug before working inside
  • Use a Residual Current Device (RCD) for additional protection
  • Ensure all equipment is properly earthed (safety earth)
  • Check cables and connectors regularly for damage

High Voltage in Equipment

Some amateur radio equipment, particularly valve (tube) amplifiers, contains dangerously high voltages (hundreds or thousands of volts) that can be present even after the equipment is switched off due to charged capacitors. Always discharge capacitors before working on such equipment.

RF Safety

Radio frequency energy can cause heating of body tissues, particularly at higher power levels and frequencies. To minimise RF exposure:

  • Keep antennas away from people — mount them as high as practically possible
  • Do not transmit while people are near the antenna
  • Use the minimum power necessary
  • Do not look into or stand in front of directional antennas (Yagi beams) while transmitting
  • Be particularly careful with VHF/UHF frequencies, which are more readily absorbed by the body

At Foundation power levels (10W), the risk is relatively low, but good practice should still be followed.

Antenna Safety

  • Never erect antennas near or where they could fall onto overhead power lines — this is extremely dangerous and frequently fatal
  • Ensure antenna supports (masts, poles) are adequately guyed and secured
  • Take care when raising and lowering antennas — have helpers and a plan
  • Consider what happens if the antenna falls — it should not be able to reach power lines or public areas
  • Wire antennas should be high enough that people cannot accidentally touch them

Lightning Protection

Antennas can attract lightning strikes. To reduce the risk:

  • Disconnect the antenna from the equipment during thunderstorms
  • Earth the antenna feeder when not in use
  • Consider fitting a lightning arrestor at the point where the feeder enters the building
  • Do not operate during thunderstorms
  • A proper RF earth is NOT the same as a lightning earth — separate systems may be needed

First Aid for Electric Shock

If someone receives an electric shock:

  1. Do not touch them if they are still in contact with the electrical source
  2. Switch off the supply if possible, or use a non-conducting object (dry wood, plastic) to separate them from the source
  3. Call 999 (or 112) for emergency services
  4. If the person is not breathing, begin CPR (if trained to do so)
  5. Place an unconscious but breathing person in the recovery position
  6. Treat any burns by cooling with clean water

PAT Testing

Portable Appliance Testing (PAT) is the process of checking electrical equipment for safety. While not legally required for personal equipment, it is good practice and may be required if you demonstrate equipment at clubs or events. A visual check and basic electrical tests are performed.

Safe Operating Practices Summary

  • Always use correctly rated fuses
  • Earth all equipment properly
  • Keep antennas away from power lines and people
  • Disconnect antennas during thunderstorms
  • Never work on live equipment
  • Use minimum necessary power
  • Know first aid procedures for electric shock

Study Tips

Safety questions are common in the exam. Know the first aid procedure (do not touch the person, switch off, call 999). Know that antennas near power lines are extremely dangerous. Understand RF safety principles. Remember the importance of proper earthing and fusing.
